approachQuestion.prompt:
Completion Windows
All jobs are available at time 0. Job i has positive duration t[i] and deadline d[i]. One processor runs chosen jobs sequentially without interruption, finishing each no later than its deadline. You may discard jobs. Return the maximum number that can be completed, not their IDs. Example: [(5,5),(2,6),(2,6),(2,6)] as (duration,deadline) → 3, by discarding the five-unit job.

1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ t[i],d[i] ≤ 1000000000. Input is read-only and unsorted. Total duration uses signed 64 bits. There are no release times, dependencies, rewards or setup costs. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200000; 1 ≤ t[i],d[i] ≤ 1000000000. Input is read-only and unsorted. Total duration uses signed 64 bits. There are no release times, dependencies, rewards or setup costs.

options.text: Sort a copy by nondecreasing deadline. Add each duration to a max-heap and to the selected total. If the total exceeds the current deadline, remove the largest selected duration and subtract it. Return the final heap size.
options.feedback: In deadline order, replacing the longest selected job preserves as many jobs as possible while minimizing their total occupied time. Before insertion the previous set was feasible, so removing one duration at least as large as the new one restores feasibility when needed.

options.text: Use the same deadline-ordered decisions, but find the longest selected duration by scanning the selected list whenever removal is required.
options.feedback: This makes the same correct exchanges but repeatedly searches a retained set whose maximum can be maintained.

options.text: Process jobs by deadline and accept each if it fits, never replacing an accepted job.
options.feedback: In the example, accepting duration 5 first causes every duration-2 job to be rejected, returning 1 rather than 3.

options.text: Sort by duration ascending and accept each job only if appending it meets its own deadline, without reordering earlier accepted jobs.
options.feedback: For [(2,100),(3,3)], this accepts the two-unit job first and rejects the other, although running the three-unit job first completes both.

When selected durations exceed the current deadline, removing the longest minimizes remaining total without reducing count more than necessary. A shorter replacement leaves at least as much room for later deadlines.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A with iterative heapsort on a copied n-record array and a binary max-heap. Let n be jobs. Each iteration inserts a duration and removes at most one maximum; all sums use constant-time 64-bit arithmetic. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Sort deadlines and insert/remove each selected duration at most once.
details: Sorting costs O(n log(n+1)). Across n jobs there are n insertions and at most n root removals, within the same bound. The copied array and selected heap each use O(n) space, even though the answer is just a count. The heap avoids rescanning chosen durations on every exchange.
“O(n²) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The fixed method does not linearly search for each longest job.
“O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Comparison sorting and heap repairs cannot be omitted.
“O(n log(n+1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Both the sorted input copy and selected durations are auxiliary storage.
